The UN GPs recommend concrete actions for states to meet their duty, including enacting and enforcing laws that require businesses to respect human rights, creating a regulatory environment that enables such respect, and providing guidance to companies on their responsibilities. ICAN commends Austria for its role in coordinating this process during this past intersessional period, and gathering the input of states and leading civil society experts to outline the legitimate security concerns of TPNW states parties, including the flaws inherent in the theory of nuclear deterrence and the extreme dangers involved in the practice and promotion of this theory. The report emphasizes that TPNW states parties see the continued possession of nuclear weapons and threats to use them as constituting a national security threat to them. It is not idealistic or naive to expect that nuclear disarmament must take place now. What is naive is the assumption that nuclear weapons will not be used, intentionally or by accident or miscalculation. leading to catastrophic and cascading consequences for all. All the warning signs are there that the status quo is untenable and unacceptable. The report dismisses as disingenuous the notion often put forth by nuclear armed states and complicit states that nuclear disarmament must wait until a certain environment exists. It is unrealistic to expect that such an ideal environment would precede nuclear disarmament. Rather, meaningful progress on disarmament is the key to creating such an environment. The report notes that while nuclear deterrence is a theory that cannot be proven, what is not disputed is that nuclear deterrence can fail and that the result will be catastrophic. To achieve our shared goal of advancing nuclear disarmament, We must first change the way nuclear weapons are talked about, and TPNW States Parties and supporters have the power to do this. The language used by nuclear deterrence proponents deliberately obfuscates the harms of threats to use nuclear weapons and the harms of continued possession of nuclear weapons. A number of nuclear-armed States use the term nuclear deterrent instead of nuclear weapons in order to shift the thinking away from the weapons and their impacts altogether. This then makes the concept of the possession of weapons of mass destruction more palatable to their domestic and international audiences. The marketing of nuclear deterrents as the guarantor of state security and even international stability has been greatly successful in separating the weapon from the catastrophic humanitarian harm it is designed to cause. Mainstream media outlets routinely use the sanitized language and imagery of nuclear weapons when they report on the subject. There has been a concerted effort to construct and embed nuclear deterrence in public discourse. And now, with the work being undertaken by TPNW states parties, there will be a concerted effort to deconstruct it. This is the logical next step in the evolution of the TPNW's role in the geopolitical landscape, and it has the potential to flip the script on nuclear weapons. ICAN urges states parties and all states to pursue the recommendations in this report including to question nuclear-armed states and their allies about their policies, frequently, at the highest levels, and across different forums, to expose the contradictions in their arguments, and to demand accountability for the risks they impose on the world. By engaging consistently in these discussions, states parties can erode the fabricated legitimacy of nuclear deterrence, and can assert the TPNW as the only framework that truly addresses the security needs of all states. Thank you.
